bees: Honeybee foragers that discover a rich patch of flowers return to the hive and perform a waggle dance on the vertical surface of the comb.
The angle of the waggle run relative to vertical encodes the direction of the food source relative to the current position of the sun.
The duration of each waggle run encodes distance, so a longer run tells recruits that the flowers are farther from the colony.
Follower bees stay in close contact with the dancer, sensing vibrations and the scent of nectar carried on her body.
For nearby food the foragers perform a round dance, which signals that flowers are close without giving a precise bearing.
Researchers verified the dance language by moving feeders and watching recruits search where the dance predicted.
volcano: Stratovolcanoes are built from alternating layers of lava flows, ash, and pyroclastic debris accumulated over many eruptions.
Viscous andesitic magma traps dissolved gases, which can drive explosive eruptions when pressure is suddenly released.
Monitoring stations track ground deformation, sulfur dioxide emissions, and swarms of small earthquakes beneath the summit.
Lahars, which are mudflows of volcanic debris and water, can travel tens of kilometers down river valleys.
Ash columns injected into the stratosphere can cool global temperatures for a year or more after a large eruption.
Hazard maps divide the surrounding land into zones based on the likely reach of flows and falling ash.
trade: Medieval merchants in the Hanseatic towns traded timber, furs, grain, and salted herring across the Baltic Sea.
Guilds regulated prices, quality, and apprenticeship, giving established traders control over who could enter a craft.
Bills of exchange allowed merchants to move value between distant fairs without carrying large amounts of coin.
Tolls on rivers and bridges were a major source of revenue for lords and a constant complaint of travelling traders.
Champagne fairs rotated through several towns each year and drew merchants from Italy, Flanders, and beyond.
Account books with double-entry records spread from Italian cities as trading houses grew larger and more complex.
